**(2) Reflection identities.** Let $a\in V$ with $B(a,a)\ne0$. **(3) The rank-two plane.** Let $s\ne t$ in $S$, put $P:=\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$ and $c:=c(s,t)$ as in [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]] (so $c=1$ when $m(s,t)=\infty$). Then:

For $w\in W$ and $f\in V^*$ the formula $(w\cdot f)(v)=f(\rho(w)^{-1}v)$ defines an element of $V^*$ because a composite of linear maps is linear, and $f\mapsto w\cdot f$ is linear because evaluation at $v$ is linear in $f$. Moreover $\mathrm{id}\cdot f=f$, since $\rho(\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}$, and $$w_1\cdot(w_2\cdot f)=f\circ\rho(w_2)^{-1}\circ\rho(w_1)^{-1}=f\circ\rho(w_1w_2)^{-1}=(w_1w_2)\cdot f,$$ using $\rho(w_1w_2)=\rho(w_1)\rho(w_2)$ and hence $\rho(w_1w_2)^{-1}=\rho(w_2)^{-1}\rho(w_1)^{-1}$.

Generators on the dual plane. The formulas in [F1] show $r_s(P)=P=r_t(P)$, since each map preserves $P$ and is its own inverse. Hence every $g\in W_{s,t}=\langle r_s,r_t\rangle$ and its inverse preserve $P$. The restriction $g\mapsto g|_P$ is a homomorphism into $\mathrm{GL}(P)$, so $(g\cdot\varphi)(v)=\varphi(g^{-1}v)$ is well-defined on $P^*$ and is a left action: $(gh)\cdot\varphi=\varphi\circ h^{-1}\circ g^{-1}=g\cdot(h\cdot\varphi)$, and the identity acts trivially. Here $s\cdot\varphi$ and $t\cdot\varphi$ denote the actions of $r_s$ and $r_t$ respectively. The dual basis vectors satisfy $(s\cdot f_s)(e_s)=f_s(\rho(s)^{-1}e_s)=f_s(-e_s)=-1$ and $(s\cdot f_s)(e_t)=f_s(\rho(s)e_t)=f_s(e_t+2ce_s)=2c$, while $(s\cdot f_t)(e_s)=f_t(-e_s)=0$ and $(s\cdot f_t)(e_t)=f_t(e_t+2ce_s)=1$; hence in coordinates $s\cdot(y_sf_s+y_tf_t)=(-y_s)f_s+(2cy_s+y_t)f_t$, that is $$\rho(s)^*(y_s,y_t)=(-y_s,\ 2cy_s+y_t).$$ The same computation with $s$ replaced by $t$ gives $\rho(t)^*(y_s,y_t)=(y_s+2cy_t,\ -y_t)$. The finite rank-two model. Assume $m<\infty$ and put $\theta:=\pi/m$ and $c=\cos\theta$. Then $0<\theta\le\pi/2$, $\sin\theta\ne0$ and $1-c^2=\sin^2\theta$. On $P$ put $u:=e_s$ and $v:=(e_t+ce_s)/\sin\theta$. Then $B(u,u)=B(e_s,e_s)=1$, $B(u,v)=(B(e_s,e_t)+cB(e_s,e_s))/\sin\theta=(-c+c)/\sin\theta=0$ and $B(v,v)=(B(e_t,e_t)+2cB(e_s,e_t)+c^2B(e_s,e_s))/\sin^2\theta=(1-2c^2+c^2)/\sin^2\theta=(1-c^2)/\sin^2\theta=1$: thus $(u,v)$ is a $B|_P$-orthonormal basis of $P$ and $e_s=u$, $e_t=-cu+\sin\theta\,v$. Since $r_s$ fixes $\ker B(-,e_s)\cap P=\mathbb Rv$ pointwise and sends $u=e_s$ to $-u$, in the coordinates $(x_u,x_v)$ of the basis $(u,v)$ it is $r_s(x_u,x_v)=(-x_u,x_v)$; since $\ker B(-,e_t)\cap P$ is spanned by $(\sin\theta,c)$ and $r_t(e_t)=-e_t$, the map $r_t$ is the reflection in the line $\mathbb R(\sin\theta,c)$. Consequently the composite $A:=r_sr_t$ satisfies $A(u)=r_s(e_s+2ce_t)=r_s\bigl((1-2c^2)u+2c\sin\theta\,v\bigr)=(2c^2-1)u+2c\sin\theta\,v=(\cos2\theta)u+(\sin2\theta)v$ and $A(v)=-\sin2\theta\,u+\cos2\theta\,v$, so in the orthonormal coordinates $$A(x_u,x_v)=(x_u\cos2\theta-x_v\sin2\theta,\ x_u\sin2\theta+x_v\cos2\theta),$$ the rotation through $2\theta$, whose order is exactly $m$.

The rank-two roots. Assume $m<\infty$ and keep the orthonormal coordinates $(u,v)$ of 1.4, in which $A$ is the rotation through $2\theta$. Then $A^k e_s=(\cos2k\theta)u+(\sin2k\theta)v$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, and $r_sA^ke_s=(-\cos2k\theta)u+(\sin2k\theta)v=(\cos(m-2k)\theta)u+(\sin(m-2k)\theta)v$ because $\pi=m\theta$ and $\cos(\pi-\alpha)=-\cos\alpha$, $\sin(\pi-\alpha)=\sin\alpha$. Moreover $e_t=-\cos\theta\,u+\sin\theta\,v=(\cos(m-1)\theta)u+(\sin(m-1)\theta)v$, and the same two formulas applied to $e_t$ give $A^ke_t$ and $r_sA^ke_t$ at angles $(m-1+2k)\theta$ and $(1-2k)\theta$. As $k$ varies over $\mathbb Z$ the angles $2k\theta$ are exactly the even multiples of $\theta$ and the angles $(1-2k)\theta$ are exactly the odd multiples, so every element of $S:=\{(\cos j\theta)u+(\sin j\theta)v:j=0,1,\dots,2m-1\}$ is one of the four displayed families and $S\subseteq\Phi_P$; conversely $S$ contains $e_s$ and $e_t$ and is stable under $A$ (which adds $2\theta$ to an angle) and under $r_s$ (which sends an angle $\varphi$ to $\pi-\varphi=(m\theta-\varphi)$), hence stable under $W_{s,t}=\langle\rho(s),\rho(t)\rangle=\langle\rho(s),A\rangle$, so $\Phi_P\subseteq S$. Therefore $$\Phi_P=W_{s,t}\{e_s,e_t\}=\{(\cos j\theta)u+(\sin j\theta)v:\ j=0,1,\dots,2m-1\},$$ a set of exactly $2m$ unit vectors, and $\Phi_P$ is stable under $\beta\mapsto-\beta$.

The infinite case. Assume $m=\infty$, so $c=1$ and by 1.2 the generators act by $s\cdot(y_s,y_t)=(-y_s,2y_s+y_t)$ and $t\cdot(y_s,y_t)=(y_s+2y_t,-y_t)$ and preserve $\delta=y_s+y_t$. On the affine line $\{\delta=1\}$ parametrized by $\tau=y_s$ these maps read $\tau\mapsto-\tau$ and $\tau\mapsto2-\tau$, the two reflections of the line about $0$ and $1$. Every word in the two involutions rewrites to $A^k$ or $A^kr_s$ with $k\in\mathbb Z$, where $A=r_sr_t$; their actions on this affine line are respectively $\tau\mapsto\tau-2k$ and $\tau\mapsto-\tau-2k$. These are pairwise distinct, so restriction to $P$ is faithful on $W_{s,t}$. The interval images are $A^k[0,1]=[-2k,1-2k]$ and $A^kr_s[0,1]=[-1-2k,-2k]$, so they are exactly $[j,j+1]$ for $j\in\mathbb Z$, with distinct elements giving distinct intervals. These cover the affine line by [F8] and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Since $C_P$ is the cone on $[0,1]$ in the half-plane $\{\delta\ge0\}$ and the action is linear, the chamber $wC_P$ is the cone on the interval corresponding to $w$; these cones have pairwise disjoint interiors and their union is $\{\varphi:\delta(\varphi)>0\}\cup\{0\}$, because every point with $\delta>0$ is a positive multiple of a unique point of $\{\delta=1\}$ lying in a unit interval, while every point of a cone on a unit interval has $\delta\ge0$ and only $0$ has $\delta=0$. By [F1] and the normal forms above, the roots are precisely the four families $A^ke_s=(1+2k,2k)$, $A^ke_t=(-2k,1-2k)$, $A^kr_se_s=(-1-2k,-2k)$ and $A^kr_se_t=(2+2k,1+2k)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$. Equivalently $\Phi_P=\{(j+1,j),(j,j+1):j\in\mathbb Z\}$, since the first and fourth families cover the even and odd values of $j$ in the first pair, and the second and third do so in the second pair. On $\{\delta=1\}$ the equation $\varphi(ae_s+be_t)=0$ is $(a-b)y_s+b=0$, so the two root families give wall traces $-j$ and $j+1$, exactly the integers. If two chamber intervals are $[j,j+1]$ and $[l,l+1]$ with $j<l$, the wall whose trace is $j+1$ places their interiors in opposite open half-planes, because its defining linear form on $\{\delta>0\}$ has the sign of $y_s/\delta-(j+1)$ up to a fixed nonzero factor.

The rank-two walls. Assume $m<\infty$. The map $\flat:P\to P^*$, $x\mapsto B(x,\cdot)$, is an isomorphism: in the orthonormal basis $(u,v)$ of 1.4 its inverse sends $\varphi$ to $\varphi(u)u+\varphi(v)v$. Moreover it intertwines the two actions, since $(g\cdot\flat(x))(z)=B(x,g^{-1}z)=B(gx,z)=\flat(gx)(z)$ for $g\in W_{s,t}$. For $\beta\in P$ one has $\flat(\beta^\perp)=H_\beta\cap P^*$, where $\beta^\perp=\{x\in P:B(x,\beta)=0\}$: indeed $\flat(x)(\beta)=B(x,\beta)$ vanishes exactly when $x\in\beta^\perp$. By 2.1 each $\beta\in\Phi_P$ is a unit vector at an angle $j\theta$, so $\beta^\perp$ is the line at angle $j\theta+\pi/2$, and the lines $H_\beta\cap P^*$ depend only on the pair $\{\beta,-\beta\}$: there are exactly $m$ of them, at angles $\pi/2+j\theta$, $j=0,\dots,m-1$, equally spaced by $\theta$. The chamber $C_P=\{\varphi\in P^*:\varphi(e_s)\ge0,\ \varphi(e_t)\ge0\}$ corresponds under $\flat$ to $\{x\in P:B(x,e_s)\ge0,\ B(x,e_t)\ge0\}$, whose boundary lines are $e_s^\perp$ (the line at angle $\pi/2$) and $e_t^\perp$ (the line at angle $(m-1)\theta+\pi/2$, i.e. $\pi/2-\theta$): so $C_P=\flat$ of the closed sector between these two consecutive walls, of angle $\theta$, and no root hyperplane line meets $C_P^\circ$ because the $m$ walls are equally spaced by $\theta$ and contain both boundary lines.

The finite chamber tiling. Assume $m<\infty$. Put $a:=r_s$, $b:=r_t$, and $A:=ab$. Since $a^2=b^2=1$ and $aAa=A^{-1}$, every word in $a,b$ rewrites to $A^k$ or $A^ka$. The finite relation $A^m=1$ therefore gives at most $2m$ elements, represented by $0\le k<m$. Their restrictions to $P$ are all distinct: the rotations $A^k|_P$ are distinct by their exact order $m$, the maps $A^ka|_P$ are distinct after cancellation of $a|_P$, and a rotation cannot equal a reflection because their determinants on $P$ are $1$ and $-1$. Thus restriction to $P$ is faithful on this matrix subgroup, $|W_{s,t}|=2m$, and it is the dihedral group of order $2m$. Its contragredient action on $P^*$ has the same distinct elements. The action maps the set of $m$ walls to itself, because $g\cdot(H_\beta\cap P^*)=H_{g\beta}\cap P^*$ for $g\in W_{s,t}$ and $\Phi_P$ is $W_{s,t}$-stable, so it permutes the $2m$ closed sectors; it maps the sector $C_P$ to the sectors obtained by successive rotations through $2\theta$ and by the reflection $\rho(s)$, which realizes all $2m$ of them: under $\flat^{-1}$, $C_P$ has angular interval $[\pi/2-\theta,\pi/2]$ and $r_sC_P$ has interval $[\pi/2,\pi/2+\theta]$; their $A^k$ images add $2k\theta$, giving all consecutive sectors modulo $2\pi$. Thus the orbit of $C_P$ is exactly the set of closed sectors cut out by the $m$ root hyperplanes. Since $|W_{s,t}|=2m$ equals the number of sectors, the action on the orbit is simply transitive, and the sectors have pairwise disjoint interiors and union $P^*$ as the $2m$ sectors of $m$ distinct lines through the origin. Finally, a sign choice for each of the $m$ wall forms defines an intersection of open half-planes. If nonempty it is convex, by linearity of those forms, and so lies in a single sector: the segment joining any two of its points meets no wall. Thus distinct sector interiors have different signs for some wall form, which supplies a root hyperplane separating their entire interiors.
